items.article_context_en: The departure of President Donald Trump's crypto adviser, Patrick Witt, leaves the digital assets office vacant and its policy aims uncertain. When President Donald Trump returned to the White House last year, he not only shed his earlier resistance to crypto technology but embraced the industry with the hiring of a high-profile crypto czar and the establishment of his President’s Council of Advisors for Digital Assets. Almost two years later, that policy push seems to have gone quiet for the moment, with the departure of Patrick Witt, who had been the final crypto adviser running that office. And when the president recently ushered in a new artificial intelligence czar, the job that was once split between crypto and AI seemed to have dropped its crypto remit. So who is minding the store for crypto policy at the White House? It's not clear, even as a handful of people on Capitol Hill continue to suggest that the final weeks of the congressional session after the November elections could still see some legislative action for the industry. The White House still has a staff of policy advisers, and Trump's administration now boasts several crypto regulatory irons in the fire at agencies such as the Securities and Exchange Commission. But no new name has been explicitly attached to Trump's in-house crypto initiatives. A White House official told CoinDesk on Thursday that Witt's work was appreciated and wished him "the best of luck in the future endeavors." The official didn’t comment on who would be taking over. "Crypto and Clarity Act will continue to be a priority for the president," the official said. The effort began several weeks before Trump returned to office in 2025, when the president-elect named David Sacks, the former PayPal executive, as his incoming AI and crypto czar. Trump also tapped a little-known former college football player, Bo Hines, to be the first director of the digital assets advisory council — at first a one-person effort, but eventually adding a deputy. Hines quickly became the crypto face of the White House, taking constant meetings with crypto insiders and appearing on event stages. And his brief tenure of about eight months concluded with a major win for the industry in Congress: the passage of the Guiding and Establishing National Innovation for U.S.

items.article_context_en: The scheme allegedly stole tens of millions through Russian-language Facebook ads and fake advisers, then went after victims again with fake recovery offers. Brooklyn prosecutors and the FBI have seized or disrupted 241 websites and 112 servers tied to a crypto investment scam that allegedly stole tens of millions of dollars from Russian-speaking victims in the U.S. The operation, carried out last week, came after a three-year investigation into a fraud network that relied on online infrastructure and IP addresses in Ukraine and other Eastern European countries, Brooklyn District Attorney Eric Gonzalez said. The scammers drew victims through Russian-language Facebook ads that promised investment opportunities. Fake advisers then called the victims and coached them to buy cryptocurrency and send it to fraudulent trading platforms. When victims tried to withdraw their funds, the platforms locked their accounts or demanded more payments for supposed taxes and fees. The scammers then “tried to exploit them again with false promises to recover their money,” Gonzalez said. Recovered data showed they contacted victims a few weeks after the initial fraud, offering to retrieve the stolen funds. The DA’s Virtual Currency Unit had previously seized or disrupted 400 domains tied to crypto investment fraud, but replacement sites kept appearing. This time, investigators targeted the servers, hosted by Eastern European and U.S. companies, that held victim data and the software used to run the fraud. The goal was to stop the operators from quickly launching new sites. The case comes as crypto investment scams accounted for roughly 84% of the $8.65 billion in investment-fraud losses reported to the FBI in 2025, according to the bureau’s annual report. Across all internet-crime categories, crypto-linked losses totaled $11.37 billion, approximately 54% of the $20.88 billion overall.

items.article_summary_en: The Ledger Atom, scheduled for release in mid-2027, marks a departure from the industry’s emphasis on safeguarding digital assets on minimalist devices meant to be locked away in a drawer or a desk. The Atom announcement comes amid fallout from a supply-chain security breach involving Malaysian distributor CryptoBilis, in which attackers reportedly tampered with devices before they reached customers. Onchain researchers estimated losses of up to $93.2 million across more than 300 wallets, with Tether freezing $10 million of its dollar-pegged stablecoin USDT tied to the theft. The compromised wallets allegedly contained hidden chips capable of intercepting users’ 24-word recovery phrases — the stream of random words that only the owner of the wallet should know as the ultimate safeguard to their digital assets — by reading signals from their screens.
items.article_context_en: Ledger’s Atom will run apps like WhatsApp and Instragram and let users switch between smartphone functions and a protected mode for managing digital assets. Cryptocurrency hardware wallet maker Ledger said it is developing a new device that looks and functions more like a smartphone than a traditional wallet. The Ledger Atom, scheduled for release in mid-2027, marks a departure from the industry’s emphasis on safeguarding digital assets on minimalist devices meant to be locked away in a drawer or a desk. The Atom runs Android, meaning users will be able to install everyday applications like WhatsApp, Instagram and TikTok. Users can switch between ordinary smartphone functionality and a protected mode for managing digital assets. The device also incorporates integration with the AI assistant OpenClaw. The product will be manufactured at Ledger’s location in Vietnam, as is customary with its more complex devices. The Atom announcement comes amid fallout from a supply-chain security breach involving Malaysian distributor CryptoBilis, in which attackers reportedly tampered with devices before they reached customers. Onchain researchers estimated losses of up to $93.2 million across more than 300 wallets, with Tether freezing $10 million of its dollar-pegged stablecoin USDT tied to the theft. The compromised wallets allegedly contained hidden chips capable of intercepting users’ 24-word recovery phrases — the stream of random words that only the owner of the wallet should know as the ultimate safeguard to their digital assets — by reading signals from their screens. The incident largely affected users in Southeast Asia, with Ledger citing research on Wednesday to show no loss of funds reported in Europe. Ledger says Atom will incorporate additional protections specifically designed to counter this type of attack, a spokesperson told CoinDesk via email. The safeguards include a protective enclosure around the device’s most sensitive components, sensors that detect attempts to remove its screen or back cover and packaging designed to reveal whether it has been opened. The tamper-detection system has its own battery to ensure it functions even if the device is switched off.

items.article_context_en: 15, 2026 Bitcoin BTC$80,955.28 has dropped more than 2% in the past 24 hours, with some of the other major coins such as XRP (XRP), ether ETH$2,448.16 and solana (SOL) sliding even further. The move looks less like a crypto-specific story and more like a broad-based exit from riskier investments. Futures tied to copper, a closely watched barometer of global economic health, fell nearly 1%, extending Wednesday's 1.6% decline. Other growth-sensitive assets tumbled, with Asian stocks dragged lower by a rout in Korean chipmakers. Nasdaq index futures and risk-sensitive currency pairs such as Aussie dollar-Swiss franc, are down as well. At the same time, Treasury yields are falling — meaning bond prices are rising — while gold is up 1%. The yield on the 10-year note, the benchmark borrowing rate, has dropped by eight basis points to 5.08%, extending the pullback from the recent peak of 5.36%. Treasuries and gold are often treated as haven investments. Together, the moves point to investors reducing exposure to risk and seeking safety, with some stagflation fears mixed in. “It feels more like a stagflationary environment where risk assets and the US dollar generally underperform, while gold outperforms,” InvestingLive analyst Giuseppe Dellamotta wrote in a market update. Concerns the Fed will raise interest rates have been cited as one catalyst after Wednesday’s hotter-than-expected U.S. But that concern appears to be fading. CME fed funds futures now price in only a 29% chance of the central bank hiking its benchmark rate into the 4%–4.25% range later this month. The remaining probability is for rates to stay unchanged at 3.75%–4%.

items.article_context_en: Australian crypto platforms must apply for an ASIC license by October 2027 to continue operating under the new regulatory framework. Australia's financial regulator proposed new standards for cryptocurrency exchanges and digital asset custodians, setting out how companies must protect customer funds, execute trades and meet financial requirements under laws that take effect next year. The Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) said it opened a consultation on the rules on Thursday, which would require affected firms to obtain or update their regulatory approval or license. 27, with final guidance and standards expected in March 2027. The proposals mark the next step in Australia’s effort to bring crypto businesses under the same regulatory framework as traditional financial firms. Parliament passed the legislation in April, joining jurisdictions such as the European Union, Singapore and Hong Kong, which have introduced dedicated crypto regulations. Australia's move comes years after the 2022 collapse of FTX left about 30,000 Australian customers unable to access their money. Three years earlier, Cryptopia, an exchange in neighboring New Zealand, went bankrupt after a major hack. The rules take effect on April 8, 2027. Crypto firms already operating in the country have until Oct. 7 of the next year to apply for a license and can continue doing business while ASIC reviews their applications. For Australian investors, the changes would mean clearer rules on how exchanges hold their assets, execute orders and handle conflicts of interest. Crypto companies would face new compliance obligations and financial requirements to operate legally in the country. "Our approach is based on the principle of 'same activity, same risk, same regulatory outcome' to align Australia with the approach of comparable overseas jurisdictions," ASIC Commissioner Alan Kirkland said.

items.article_context_en: Ether accounted for nearly 60% of the forced closures across the two largest cryptocurrencies, falling roughly twice as much as bitcoin. Nearly $483 million in bitcoin and ether futures positions were closed over the past 24 hours as cryptocurrency prices fell Thursday, with ether traders taking the largest hit. Crypto losses worsened on Thursday morning as uncertainty over the Federal Reserve’s next interest-rate decision weighed on markets. Bitcoin traded around $81,000, down roughly 3% over 24 hours, while ether lost more than 6% to about $2,350. XRP and Solana’s SOL fell around 5%, and dogecoin dropped roughly 6%. Ether contracts accounted for about $286 million of liquidations, compared with $197 million for bitcoin, according to CoinGlass data checked during Asian morning hours. Ether fell about 6.4% to $2,356, while bitcoin lost roughly 3.2% to trade around $81,000. Liquidations happen when traders use borrowed money and a price move leaves them without enough collateral to keep their bets open. The exchange closes the position automatically. Someone using $1,000 to control a $10,000 position, for example, can lose their backing on a move of less than 10% against them. Those closures can add pressure to a falling market, forcing traders out regardless of whether they wanted to sell at that price. Ether’s damage was larger even though its futures market is considerably smaller. Outstanding ether contracts totaled about $30 billion, against $52 billion for bitcoin. The liquidation figures measure the value of positions closed, rather than the cash traders personally lost.
